doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Unified field theory: rhythm and phrasing as the key
summary: He explains the 'Countdown' common-note approach and says rhythm and phrasing unify his thinking.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: beats — so the harmony is moving at a quick pace. It’s not there for four bars, eight bars. But it’s moving every two bars. And the tempo is at a good clip. So there is a way that you have to look at all of that harmonic minutiae and there’s a way that you have to look at a broader arc over that, which means you really do have to have your ears on and think melodically at the same time that you’re adhering to time and space. So here again you’re really walking and chewing gum at the same time. And see here’s where all of this perception and how you’re looking at things come in. Now everybody’s different and there’s a lot of ways to look at music. You can look at music rhythmically only, harmonically only, or melodically only. But the real deal is amalgamating all of that into one homogeneous behavior and then so therefore having the output be whatever it is. But see there again lies this different — different ways to think. And everybody’s different. Yeah. So this is what Barry meant by you can’t be a C student with some of this stuff here. You know? This is some stuff you’ve got to deal with. Now having said that there’s also this part of the equation. The subconscious mind, who we are as human beings and people. Already here is every note that we’ve — we’ve heard every note it is. Because this big piece of meat is the greatest computer in the world. There’s only twelve notes. We’ve heard every one of them since we came out of — since we pop out of the womb. We’ve heard them. Okay we’ve heard rhythms, we’ve heard chords — whether we know what to think about them, how to think of them, it’s already there. So a lot of times success is based on what part of the mind, or what kind of mentation should I put in play to get the best results, and therein goes the four dimensional chess again and how people think you know, and you’ve got the variety of personality and then I can only say how I approach it. I’m sure other people approach it another way. But see yet again, I’ll look at all of that and realize say a tune like “Countdown” where the harmony is moving very quickly, but I will still — part of my way of thinking is what are some of the common notes with all of that harmonic movement. Because they can be moving quickly and changing quickly but there are certain common notes that’s connecting all of them or at least some of them. So your melodic ear has to be on. And see your cognitive mind, your analytical mind has to understand the form and structure of what’s actually going on. But how you artistically behave is a whole ‘nother game. That’s another part of the mind. The analytical part will just say oh, you know it’s “Countdown” so it’s going up a minor third and then it’s going to the fourth and then another minor third. You can get into all of that technical stuff and musical harmony and theory and all that. But how do you behave with that. Spend time — with time and space in real time and be creative. And that’s really something. But the way I look at things, I try to look for what I call as best as possible a “unified field theory.” Kind of what Einstein was looking for, a “unified field theory.” What is the equation that really kind of nails the whole shebang? And maybe there’s no

such thing, maybe there is. But I always try to look at what is the one thing that I can maybe — the form of mentation that might give me the best results. Is there one thing, of all of the many things and ways to think of things, what is the one thing that will amalgamate all these moving parts and all these brain departments and functionality. And then for me it’s rhythm. Rhythm. Phrasing. That’s for me. And my melodic ear is on. It’s on, I have it on. There are certain things that I would say is static. They’re always on. These ears are always open. They’re never off. They shouldn’t be. They should be always on. And then the rest is like phrasing it and the rhythmic aspect, rhythmic configurations. How do you phrase what you hear? And see rhythm has almost the last thing to say about it because you can hear anything. You might be — people who have perfect pitch, they can identify what they’re hearing. Say well this is A, this is D or this is a A minor or this is a G seventh. They can tell you that without even thinking about it because they’ve got perfect pitch, whatever that means. They can tell you that. But how do you behave with that? How do you phrase that? There is a whole different thing right there, see? So this is like — what is the one thing that I could bring all these different mental functionalities together so that I could behave in a way that I’m musically successful. And then for me I — for me it’s almost like the phrasing and the rhythm. Because I can hear what’s going on. Fine. But how do I phrase it? And what is the rhythmic configuration of what I’m hearing? I can play a whole note, I can play a half note, I can play sixteenth notes. I can play any configuration I want. But what am I? Or how am I going to slice this hearing into parts? And what’s the boss? What’s telling me what note when? What’s telling me? So I have a way of looking at music like what, where, when. So I’ll use language as a metaphor. What, where, when. What is whatever the note is. Whatever the chord is. Whatever the sound is. Is it a diminished? Is it half-diminished? Is it major? Is it this, is it that. When and where is how do you sequence and geographically distribute what into these smaller pieces. And when is the rhythmic, the time and space aspect. When. You know when, what, where. You know when, what, where. So it’s all three in it. All three. Now which one is more important/less important? And guess what? They’re all equally important. Because what is meaningless. Where you put what is meaningless. And everything is time and space, according to some point of reference. Everything.
